title: Beauty and ugliness together
hookLine: when all know beauty as beauty, ugliness appears; the sage teaches without words (Tao Te Ching 2)
last: NOT THE ONE THAT CAN BE TOLD.

cards: A grandmother at a stove. She has never once given a cooking lesson. No recipe card, no lecture on salt.
But a child stands at her elbow most evenings, watching her hands: the pinch, the stir, the way she tastes and waits and tastes again.

Years later that child cooks the same dish, the hands move the same way, and nobody remembers being taught. Chapter two of the Tao Te Ching ends on that kind of teaching. It gets there by way of beauty, and its shadow.

teach.b: First, beauty makes ugliness. Legge's translation opens: "All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful," and in knowing it, they also get the idea of ugliness.
Crown one thing beautiful and you've drawn a line; everything on the other side becomes the ugly. Name the skillful, and the clumsy appear.
Second, pairs that need each other. The chapter lists them: what is and what isn't, hard and easy, long and short, high and low, notes and tones that make harmony together, front and back.
Each half is only known by the other. That's not a complaint about the world. It's how naming works: every word comes with its opposite attached.
Third, without the use of speech. So what does the wise person do?

In Legge's words, the sage "manages affairs without doing anything, and conveys his instructions without the use of speech." Not lazy: without forcing, without the extra layer of pointing, labeling and grading.
The teaching is in how the work is done.
The sage does the work and doesn't claim it, the chapter says, and because nothing is claimed, nothing is taken away. A grandmother doesn't sign the dish. It goes on being made anyway.

how: In Taoist teaching, the sage's 'teaching without words' is often read as teaching by example: a teacher who lives the Way so that students learn from watching rather than from instruction.

games.q: what does “beauty and ugliness together” mean?
o: a saying that beauty fades as people age
naming beauty brings ugliness along with it
a rule that ugly things should be hidden

games.q: chapter two's pairs: tap the partners.
p: teaches without the use of speech

s: chapter two says beauty and ugliness are known only through each other
in knowing the beauty of the beautiful, the world gets the idea of ugliness too.
managing affairs without doing anything means being lazy
it means without forcing, without the extra pointing and grading: the teaching is in how the work is done.
the sage in chapter two signs his work so it will last
the sage doesn't claim the work, and because nothing is claimed, nothing is taken away.

games.q: you want the people around you to learn patience. you're the sage of chapter two. what do you do?
o: give a short speech about patience.
post a list of rules about patience.
be patient, and say nothing about it.
games.why: the sage "conveys his instructions without the use of speech": the teaching is in how the work is done.

practice: Think of one thing you'd like the people around you to learn: patience in traffic, the phone down at dinner, a thank-you at the counter.

Instead of planning what to say about it, picture yourself simply doing it, quietly, with nobody told, and hold that picture while you breathe. If you pray, you can ask for help with it; if not, rehearse it in your body.

wordCard.voice: Beauty and ugliness together. Chapter two's warning that every name brings its opposite with it, and its picture of a teacher who teaches without words. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, bù yán zhī jiào: the teaching of not speaking, the teaching without words, from Tao Te Ching 2.

carryVoice: Your line: without words. The dish gets passed on, and nobody signs it. Until tomorrow.
